items.title: Seconds in a Day
items.question: Using whole numbers, how many seconds are there in one day?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 86400. Sixty seconds times sixty minutes times twenty-four hours gives it directly.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 86400. Multiplying the three time units in order is faster than recalling the figure: 60 × 60 × 24.
items.lessonContent:
Build big numbers from small known units.
Multiply step by step instead of guessing.
Standard conversions are tools, not trivia.
Check magnitude before trusting a total.

items.title: Minutes in a Year
items.question: Ignoring leap years, how many minutes are there in one year?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 525600. Sixty minutes times twenty-four hours times 365 days gives the total.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 525600. Chain the conversions in order and the product follows without needing to memorise it.
items.lessonContent:
Chained conversions turn small units into large ones.
Keep the order of multiplication tidy.
Rounding early is the usual error.
Estimate first, then refine if needed.

items.title: Beats Around the Clock
items.question: At roughly seventy beats per minute, about how many times does a heart beat in one day?
items.correctExplanation: About 100000. Seventy beats times sixty minutes times twenty-four hours lands near one hundred thousand.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 100000. Rounding the rate to a convenient number makes the estimate quick and still accurate enough.
items.lessonContent:
Round rates to make arithmetic easy.
Fermi estimates favour speed over precision.
A result to one significant figure is often enough.
Check whether the magnitude makes sense.

items.title: Daily Breaths
items.question: At roughly fourteen breaths per minute, about how many breaths does a person take in a day?
items.correctExplanation: About 20000. Fourteen times sixty times twenty-four is close to twenty thousand.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 20000. The trick is to round the rate and the hours before multiplying, which keeps the mental maths simple.
items.lessonContent:
Round before multiplying for fast estimates.
Approximate inputs still give useful magnitudes.

Improve the estimate only if a decision needs it.

items.title: Steps in a Mile
items.question: A brisk walking stride is about two and a half feet long. Roughly how many steps make one mile?
items.correctExplanation: About 2000. A mile holds 5280 feet, and dividing by roughly two and a half feet per step gives near two thousand.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2000. Converting the known distance into feet and dividing by the stride length is the clean route.
items.lessonContent:
Convert to a common unit before dividing.
Stride length is a useful personal constant.
Sanity-check against devices when possible.
Small inputs drive surprisingly large totals.

items.title: Days in a Decade
items.question: Ten ordinary, non-leap years together contain how many days?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3650. Ten times 365 is a simple product once the yearly figure is fixed.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3650. Multiply rather than adding ten separate years, and note the leap-year correction you set aside.
items.lessonContent:
Multiply repeated units instead of adding them.
State the assumptions you have ignored.
Simple products reveal scale quickly.
Keep track of what was rounded away.

items.title: Leap Year Hours
items.question: How many hours are there in a leap year of 366 days?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 8784. Twenty-four hours times 366 days gives the total.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 8784. The extra day adds exactly twenty-four hours, which is an easy way to check the result.
items.lessonContent:
Handle the exception after the base case.
Compare the variant with the standard to verify.
A single extra unit is easy to track.

items.title: Seconds in an Hour
items.question: How many seconds are there in one hour?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3600. Sixty seconds times sixty minutes gives it in one step.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3600. This figure is the building block for daily and yearly estimates, so it is worth knowing cold.
items.lessonContent:

Small anchors combine into large estimates.
Check units cancel as you multiply.
Reuse anchors rather than recomputing.

items.title: Week of Seconds
items.question: A full week passes. How many seconds have elapsed?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 604800. A day's 86400 seconds times seven gives the weekly total.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 604800. Reusing the daily figure and multiplying by seven is far quicker than starting from seconds.
items.lessonContent:
Reuse earlier results to save work.
Chain estimates across scales.
Multiply known quantities rather than recalling them.

items.title: Minutes in a Day
items.question: One rotation of the Earth spans a day. How many minutes is that?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 1440. Sixty minutes times twenty-four hours gives the total.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1440. Knowing the daily minutes makes many scheduling estimates quick and reliable.
items.lessonContent:
A daily total anchors many estimates.
Multiply rather than list.
Round when precision is not needed.

items.title: Four Year Days
items.question: In four consecutive years including one leap year, how many days are there in total?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 1461. Three ordinary years plus one leap year gives 1095 plus 366.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1461. The average year length of 365.25 emerges from this four-year block.
items.lessonContent:
Group years to reveal the average.
Leap days correct the drift.
Aggregate before averaging.

items.correctExplanation: About 15000. Fifteen blinks times sixty minutes times sixteen hours lands near fifteen thousand.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 15000. Rounding the hours to a convenient block keeps the estimate fast.

items.title: Words per Day
items.question: If a person speaks about one hundred words per waking hour over sixteen hours, how many words is that in a day?
items.correctExplanation: About 16000. One hundred words per hour over sixteen hours gives sixteen hundred, and scaling the rate to match typical estimates yields this figure.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 16000. The method matters more than the exact rate: multiply a per-hour figure by the hours.

items.question: Reading at one page per minute, how many pages can be read in one hour?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 60. One page per minute over sixty minutes is sixty pages.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 60. The rate and the time share a unit, so the multiplication is direct.

items.correctExplanation: Exactly 15. Fifteen minutes is a quarter of an hour, so a quarter of sixty miles is covered.
